lesson.child_mission: Waterproof materials keep water out; absorbent materials soak water in. Test with drops on scrap samples and record what happens.
lesson.evidence_instructions: Save the independent response, specific revisions and both short-answer explanations; record oral evidence for speaking tasks.
lesson.extension: Apply the same science idea to a new object or material, then compare two pieces of evidence for strength.
lesson.guided_practice:
PRACTISE BEFORE READING THE FEEDBACK
Predict and test (adult help): sandwich bag; kitchen sponge; cardboard. Waterproof, absorbent, or mixed?

FEEDBACK
Bag waterproof; sponge absorbent; cardboard partly absorbent then softens.

WATCH FOR
Pouring cups of water on furniture is unsafe and unnecessary for the test.
lesson.independent_task:
INDEPENDENT EVIDENCE
Test eight scrap materials with three drops each. Record prediction, result and waterproof/absorbent/mixed. Name the best material for a rain hat and why.

Write a short reflection naming one observation or step you corrected and why.
lesson.learning_intention: Waterproof materials keep water out; absorbent materials soak water in. Test with drops on scrap samples and record what happens.
materials: Optional: safe everyday objects for observation
lesson.offline_alternative: Use paper and pencil to complete the original task, then retain a photograph or short parent observation as evidence.

Waterproof materials keep water out; absorbent materials soak water in. Test with drops on scrap samples and record what happens.

WHY IT MATTERS
This helps the learner base claims on observation, fair tests and design evidence, rather than guessing from a picture alone. Keep every claim linked to what was seen or measured.
